messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The hurricane had taken everything in a matter of hours. Mariana remembered the water rising through her ground-floor apartment in Houston, the way the furniture began to float, the sound of her neighbor Elena calling for help before the line went silent. She had climbed to the attic and stayed there, neck-deep in dark water, for nearly seven hours before the rescue boat came. By then, Elena had drowned. That was three years ago, and Mariana, now fifty-seven, had not spoken of it to anyone until she walked into the clinic.

She worked as a physical therapist at a rehabilitation center, a job she had loved for decades. But the work had become a landscape of hidden traps. When a patient mentioned a spouse named Elena, Mariana felt her stomach turn. When she walked past the therapy pool and caught the scent of chlorine and damp tile, the nausea would rise. And when the spring rains began—the sound of water hitting the roof, the sight of a flooded parking lot—her chest would tighten and the memory would surge back unbidden, not as a story she owned but as a wave of horror that seemed to belong to someone else. The memory of that night felt alien, as though it had happened to a different woman, yet the emotion was unmistakably hers: a grief so heavy it left her breathless. Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light.

That grief arrived without warning. Sometimes Mariana would be standing at a patient's bedside, adjusting a brace or demonstrating an exercise, when a feeling of overwhelming loss would wash over her—no image, no narrative, just the raw emotion of that night. She had learned to dissociate deliberately during these moments. She would fix her gaze on a point in the distance and try to will herself out of her body, to float above the scene until the feeling passed. Other times, she would dwell on how she used to be before the event—the woman who had loved the rain, who had hosted Sunday dinners, who had not been afraid of her own mind. This dwelling only brought the memories back more vividly, and soon she found herself caught in a loop: a trigger would surface, the memory would intrude, and she would try to escape it by leaving her body or losing herself in the past, which in turn made the memory feel more present and more alien all at once.

The threat never left her. She had trouble falling asleep most nights, and when she did, she woke at the smallest sound—a car door, a gust of wind—her heart pounding, convinced the water was rising again. She had come to believe that safety existed in only a very limited number of places: her bedroom, the back office at work, her car. Anywhere else felt exposed. This constant hypervigilance made her more sensitive to triggers. When a loud truck rumbled past the clinic, she would flinch, and the flinch would prime her for the next cue—the name, the smell, the sight of rain—so that even a minor trigger could set the entire cycle in motion.

Avoidance had reshaped her life. She stopped going out after work. She declined invitations from colleagues. She took the longest route home to avoid a bridge that crossed the river. But staying inside her safe zones did not quiet the memory; it only made the memory more dominant, more urgent. And the more she stayed inside, the more triggers accumulated—the sound of the faucet, the sight of the bathtub, the name of a character on television who happened to be called Elena.

What finally brought her to seek help was the grief. She had been standing in the supply closet at work when the feeling hit her without any image—just the full weight of loss, the neighbor she could not save, the home she had built, the life she had lived before. She had dissociated right there, leaning against the shelves, and when she came back she found she had been standing still for twenty minutes. Her supervisor had asked if she was okay. Mariana had said she was fine, but she knew she was not. She was tired of feeling like the memory belonged to someone else while the pain belonged entirely to her.
